title: The Roman world
seoTitle: The Roman World of Paul: What It Was Really Like
description: A long, sourced portrait of the Roman world the first churches lived in: roads, ships and cities, Caesar and the law, the household and the patron, the gods and the emperor, clubs and meals, work and the crowded city, letters, and how the church looked from outside.
line: The empire Paul crossed on foot and by ship: its roads and cities, its law and its gods, its households and its meals, with the evidence named as we go.
intro: This is a portrait of the Roman world the first churches lived in, roughly from the reign of Augustus to the early second century: the world of Acts, of Paul's letters and of Revelation. It does not argue one point. It tries to show how people traveled, worked, ate, worshiped, wrote and were judged, so that the letters of the New Testament read like what they are: mail, carried down real roads to real cities, read aloud to people who lived in rented rooms and served in other people's houses.

Each part names its evidence as it goes. For this world there is a great deal of it: Roman historians and letter writers, laws, coins, thousands of inscriptions cut in stone, and papyrus letters from the dry sands of Egypt. Much of it was written by and for the rich, so it tells us more about senators than about the slaves and day laborers who filled most of the churches. Some of the best evidence also comes from a generation or two after Paul. Where a source is later, this portrait says so. Where historians disagree, or the evidence is thin, it says that too.

One more thing before the first part. "Roman" here does not mean one people. The empire held Greeks, Syrians, Egyptians, Jews, Gauls, Africans and many others, most of whom never saw Rome and few of whom were Roman citizens. Greek, not Latin, was the common language of the eastern cities where the churches began. The people in these pages are described as their own words and remains describe them: farmers, sailors, slaves, magistrates and parents with their own gods and their own fears, not painted villains or plaster saints.

parts.title: Roads, ships and cities
parts.line: An empire wrapped around one sea, crossed on foot at about thirty kilometers a day and by ship when the weather allowed.
body: In Paul's day the empire ran from Spain to Syria and from the Rhine to the edge of the Sahara, and at its center lay not a city but a sea. Almost every place in the New Testament outside Galilee and Judea sits near the Mediterranean or on a road that leads to it. Rome held this ring of coasts with an army, a network of governors and a system of roads built first for soldiers and officials. Milestones marked the distances. Bridges, way stations and inns grew up along them. Anyone could walk them: merchants, pilgrims, slaves sent on errands, and a traveling tentmaker with a few companions.

Walking was slow. The Stanford ORBIS project, a model of travel in the Roman world built by Walter Scheidel and Elijah Meeks, assumes about thirty kilometers a day on foot for an ordinary traveler, and its makers admit there is little direct evidence for the figure. At that pace the road from one city to the next could take a week, and a letter or a friend could be a month away. The road was also dangerous. Paul's own list of hardships includes rivers, bandits, the city and the open country (2 Corinthians 11:26). In Macedonia he followed one of the great roads of the empire, the Via Egnatia, which crossed the Balkans from the Adriatic toward the Aegean. Acts names its towns in order: Neapolis on the coast, Philippi, then Amphipolis and Apollonia on the way to Thessalonica (Acts 16:11-12; 17:1).

The sea was faster and cheaper, and it was where people died. Ships kept to a season. Vegetius, a Roman writer of the late fourth century, long after Paul, gives the rule sailors had inherited: the safest sailing ran from late May to mid-September, the risky months lay on either side, and from about 11 November to 10 March the sea was treated as closed. Some historians, such as Julian Beresford in The Ancient Sailing Season (2013), have shown that ships did sail in winter when profit or need pushed them, so the rule was a habit, not a law. Acts 27 shows the habit at work. The voyage to Rome was already dangerous "because it was after the Fast," the Day of Atonement in the autumn, and Paul warned that pressing on would cost the ship and the cargo (Acts 27:9-10). The ship was an Alexandrian vessel bound for Italy, probably part of the grain trade that fed Rome, and it carried 276 people (Acts 27:6, 37). After the wreck on Malta the company waited three months and then sailed in another Alexandrian ship whose figurehead was the Twin Brothers, Castor and Pollux, the gods sailors prayed to in a storm (Acts 28:11).

The cities at the ends of these roads each had their own character. Corinth had been destroyed by Rome in 146 BC and lay mostly empty for a century until Julius Caesar refounded it in 44 BC as a Roman colony. The geographer Strabo says it was settled largely with freed slaves (Geography 8.6.23); Dorota Pawlak and others think the settlers were more mixed than that from the start. By Paul's day it was rich, new and status-hungry, with two harbors, Lechaeum on one gulf and Cenchreae on the other, which is where Phoebe served the church (Romans 16:1). Philippi was a colony of another kind. After the battle fought on its plain in 42 BC, Rome settled discharged soldiers there, and the city prided itself on being Rome in miniature. Acts calls it "the Roman colony of Philippi," and the charge against Paul there was teaching customs "unlawful for us Romans" (Acts 16:12, 21).

Ephesus was the great city of the province of Asia, a port at the mouth of the Cayster river, home of the famous temple of Artemis. Its theater, cut into the side of a hill and enlarged in later centuries, held something over twenty thousand people at its largest by most modern estimates, and that is where the crowd ran shouting in Acts 19. Thessalonica, the capital of Macedonia, was a Greek city that ran its own affairs under its own magistrates. Luke calls its officials by an unusual title, politarchs (Acts 17:6, translated "city officials"), and inscriptions from Macedonia use the same title, among them one from an old arch over the Via Egnatia in Thessalonica, now in the British Museum, whose exact date is argued.

And then there was Rome itself, the largest city anyone in the empire had seen. Nobody counted its people. Estimates by modern historians run from about half a million to a million or more, many of them crowded into tall blocks of rented rooms. Augustus tried to limit new buildings along the public streets to seventy feet, according to Strabo (Geography 5.3.7), which says something about how high and unsafe they had grown. When Paul finally arrived as a prisoner, believers walked down the Appian Way to meet him at the Forum of Appius and the Three Taverns, two stopping places south of the city (Acts 28:15). The church in Rome was already there before any apostle arrived. Paul wrote to it before he saw it.

read.text: We sailed from Troas straight to Samothrace, and the following day on to Neapolis. From there we went to the Roman colony of Philippi, the leading city of that district of Macedonia. And we stayed there several days.
read.note: Luke's travel notes read like a road log: Troas, the island of Samothrace, the port of Neapolis, then the colony of Philippi. A modern reader skims them. For the first readers they marked days at sea and days on foot along a Roman road, and they named a city that called itself Roman and would soon treat these travelers as foreigners.

read.text: By now much time had passed, and the voyage had already become dangerous because it was after the Fast. So Paul advised them, “Men, I can see that our voyage will be filled with disaster and great loss, not only to ship and cargo, but to our own lives as well.”
read.note: "After the Fast" is a date. It means autumn, when every sailor knew the safe season was ending. Paul's warning was not a vision but the kind of judgment an experienced traveler would make. The centurion trusted the pilot and the owner instead, which is what most people would have done, and the rest of the chapter is the cost.

read.text: From there we weighed anchor and came to Rhegium. After one day, a south wind came up, and on the second day we arrived at Puteoli. There we found some brothers who invited us to spend the week with them. And so we came to Rome. The brothers there had heard about us and traveled as far as the Forum of Appius and the Three Taverns to meet us. When Paul saw them, he was encouraged and gave thanks to God.
read.note: Puteoli was the great harbor where grain ships from Alexandria unloaded for Rome. From there the road ran north, and believers came out along it to meet a prisoner. In a world where travel was slow and costly, walking out to meet someone was a public act of honor. They gave it to a man in chains.

parts.title: Caesar, governors and the law
parts.line: Who ruled, who judged, what a citizen could claim, and why the cross was kept for slaves and rebels.
body: Five emperors span the New Testament. Augustus ruled from 27 BC to AD 14, Tiberius to 37, Gaius, known as Caligula, to 41, Claudius to 54 and Nero to 68. Most people in the provinces never saw any of them. What they saw was the governor. Some provinces were run by a proconsul, a senator chosen for a year, and Acts names two: Sergius Paulus on Cyprus and Gallio in Achaia, the province of Corinth (Acts 13:7; 18:12). Others were run by the emperor's own appointees, and small or troubled regions such as Judea had a prefect or procurator, which is why Paul was held for two years by Felix and then tried before Porcius Festus (Acts 24:27). Below the governor, each city ran its own business through its own council and magistrates, collected its own dues and kept its own peace. Rome stepped in when order or money was at stake.

One of those governors gives the New Testament its firmest date. At Delphi in Greece, fragments of a letter from the emperor Claudius were found cut in stone, and the letter names Gallio as proconsul. It was written during Claudius's twenty-sixth acclamation as emperor, a count the Romans kept, which falls between early AD 51 and the summer of 52. A proconsul usually served one year, so most scholars place Gallio in Corinth in 51 to 52; some argue for 50 to 51. Gallio was the brother of the philosopher Seneca. In Acts he refuses to judge a dispute he calls one of "words and names and your own law" and drives the accusers from his judgment seat (Acts 18:14-16). His year in office is the peg on which most chronologies of Paul's life hang.

Roman citizenship was a legal standing, not a nationality, and in the eastern provinces only a minority held it. It came by birth, by grant from an emperor or general, by finishing service in the auxiliary army, or by being freed by a citizen master. It protected the body. A citizen was not to be flogged or bound without trial, and he could appeal against a magistrate's sentence. How seriously Romans took this shows in Cicero's prosecution of Verres, a corrupt governor of Sicily, in 70 BC. Cicero tells how Verres had a man named Gavius beaten with rods in the forum of Messana while the only words he could say were that he was a Roman citizen, and then had him crucified, in a speech designed to make a Roman jury feel the outrage (Against Verres 2.5.161-170). In Philippi, Paul and Silas were stripped, beaten with rods and jailed by magistrates who had not asked, and the next morning those magistrates were "alarmed" to learn they had flogged citizens (Acts 16:22-23, 38).

How did anyone prove it? From the time of Augustus, from AD 4, a citizen could register a child's birth before an official and receive a wooden tablet, folded like a book, recording the declaration; the legal historian Fritz Schulz studied these in 1942. Registration was not compulsory, and Acts never says how Paul showed his status. It does show that status could be bought. The commander in Jerusalem tells Paul, "I paid a high price for my citizenship," and Paul answers, "But I was born a citizen" (Acts 22:28). The historian Cassius Dio says that under Claudius citizenship was sold through the empress Messalina and the imperial freedmen, dear at first and later so cheap it became a joke (Roman History 60.17). The commander's name, Claudius Lysias (Acts 23:26), fits a man who took the emperor's name when he became a citizen, though that is an inference. Some scholars doubt Paul was a citizen at all, because his own letters never mention it. Many others, following A. N. Sherwin-White's Roman Society and Roman Law in the New Testament (1963), find that Acts gets the legal details of the period right.

The appeal to Caesar was the citizen's last protection. When Festus seemed ready to send Paul back to Jerusalem for trial, Paul said, "I appeal to Caesar," and Festus, after consulting his council, answered, "To Caesar you will go" (Acts 25:11-12). King Agrippa later remarked that Paul could have been released if he had not appealed (Acts 26:32). About sixty years later the same practice appears in a governor's letter. Pliny the Younger, governing Bithynia around AD 112, wrote to the emperor Trajan that some accused Christians were Roman citizens, and that he had marked them to be sent to Rome (Letters 10.96).

At the bottom of Roman justice stood the cross. It was a punishment for slaves, for bandits and for rebels against Roman rule, a death meant to be slow, public and shaming. Martin Hengel's short book Crucifixion (1977) gathered the ancient evidence. After the slave revolt led by Spartacus was crushed in 71 BC, the historian Appian says six thousand captives were crucified along the road from Capua to Rome (Civil Wars 1.120). Cicero, defending a citizen in court, said the very word cross should be kept far from a Roman citizen's body, thoughts, eyes and ears (For Rabirius 16). Citizens condemned to death were usually executed by other means. That is the background to Paul's words that Christ took "the form of a servant" and became obedient to death, "even death on a cross" (Philippians 2:7-8). The phrase was not a pious ornament. It named the lowest death the empire knew.

read.text: But Paul said to the officers, “They beat us publicly without a trial and threw us into prison, even though we are Roman citizens. And now do they want to send us away secretly? Absolutely not! Let them come themselves and escort us out!”
read.note: Paul waits until morning to mention his citizenship, and then refuses to leave quietly. The magistrates of a proud Roman colony had broken Roman law in public. By making them come and escort him out, he protected the small church he was leaving behind, which would have to go on living in that city.

read.text: The commander went to Paul and asked, “Tell me, are you a Roman citizen?” “Yes,” he answered. “I paid a high price for my citizenship,” said the commander. “But I was born a citizen,” Paul replied.
read.note: Two men compare papers in a barracks. One bought his standing; the other was born to it. In a world that ranked everyone, the exchange matters, and Paul uses it. The same man would write that in Christ "there is neither Jew nor Greek, slave nor free" (Galatians 3:28). He used the empire's ranks when they could protect the gospel, and denied them any final weight.

read.text: Paul replied, “I am standing before the judgment seat of Caesar, where I ought to be tried. I have done nothing wrong to the Jews, as you yourself know very well. If, however, I am guilty of anything worthy of death, I do not refuse to die. But if there is no truth to their accusations against me, no one has the right to hand me over to them. I appeal to Caesar!” Then Festus conferred with his council and replied, “You have appealed to Caesar. To Caesar you will go!”
read.note: "I appeal to Caesar" is a legal formula, and it moved Paul's case out of a provincial court to the emperor's. It also carried him toward Rome, where he had long wanted to go. The empire's own law became the road the gospel traveled on, though no one in the room meant it that way.
